content.theory:
Objects group related data and behavior under one name — the most important data structure in JavaScript.

### Object literals
```js
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  age: 36,
  city: "London",
  greet() {
    console.log(`Hi, I'm ${this.name}`);
  }
};

console.log(user.name);        // Ada
console.log(user["age"]);      // 36
user.greet();                  // Hi, I'm Ada
```

### Add / change / delete properties
```js
user.job = "Programmer";       // add
user.age = 37;                  // change
delete user.city;               // remove
```

### Destructuring — unpack properties in one line
```js
const { name, age } = user;
console.log(name, age);   // Ada 36
```

### Spread — clone and extend
```js
const copy = { ...user, active: true };
```

### Arrays of objects — the real world
```js
const players = [
  { name: "Aria", hp: 100 },
  { name: "Blake", hp: 85 }
];

const names = players.map(p => p.name);      // ["Aria", "Blake"]
const full = players.find(p => p.hp === 100); // the first object
```

### Optional chaining — safe access
```js
console.log(user.address?.street);   // undefined, no crash
```

### this
Inside a method, `this` refers to the object the method was called on. Use regular `function`/method shorthand for `this`, and be careful using it inside arrow functions nested in methods.

exercise.instruction: Write a script: create 'hero' = { name: 'Aria', hp: 100 }. Add a method hit(damage) that reduces this.hp. Call hero.hit(25), then set output.textContent to hero.name + ' hp ' + hero.hp. Expected: 'Aria hp 75'.
hints: Hint 1: const hero = { name: "Aria", hp: 100, hit(damage) { this.hp -= damage; } };

quiz.question: What does destructuring `const { name } = user` do?
options: Pulls the name property into a variable

quiz.question: Inside a method, what does this refer to?
options: The object the method was called on
